title: Atlantic Records confusion over Barefootin'
summary: Atlantic thought Barefootin' was theirs under a deal; threats of a lawsuit came to nothing, and NOLA distributed it itself.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Was Atlantic Records involved at all?
We leased it to Atlantic Records. You did? No. Well we didn't. How that worked out? We did something.
Ehrlich said that you had some kind of deal with Atlantic, I think it was.

Yeah, but that wasn't the one that we had to deal with. This came back, we were late in the game, that with this Walker fellow, we had a record of something called, uh, uh, Pelican, or was it Pelican? We had a group, some of the same people called Pelican, and he had his own label, the Walker fellow had his own label. Eli Walker, is it Eli Walker? Eli Walker, that's him. I was saying Sigmo, where that came from. Sigmo was a bass player. Uh, Walker did, no, I'm ahead of myself again. We did Barefootin' for this fellow, and Atlantic Records thought it was for, I think we had a three record deal or something like that with them, and they thought it was their record and we, they didn't prosecute or anything like that, but it really was for Welly Eugene, Eugene Welly.
I think Ehrlich said that there was a lawsuit over, or they were gonna?

Or they were going to, I believe. Uh-huh. And, uh, whatever happened, it happened, but there was no kind of, uh, there was nothing with it, you know. Uh-huh. Now, if they had the record, I'd forgotten who, I think we distributed it ourselves, or not we, I think. And you were NOLA. NOLA. Through cars. Through cars. Absolutely.
And that's what, they thought it was our record because it was on our label and we just proved that it wasn't our record. But there was no kind of, uh, other than the threatening.
